summary: Describes the guidelines and procedures for forming and operating IETF working groups, including the formal relationship between working groups and the Internet Engineering Steering Group. It is informational. It was replaced by RFC 2418.

eli5.summary: Rules for how small teams in the IETF get started and do their work. A newer rulebook replaced it.

subtitle: The 1994 rulebook for how IETF working groups are formed, run, and wound down.

tldr.problem: The IETF had grown too large to run on informality alone, and people forming or chairing working groups needed written guidance on how to proceed.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes how a working group is chartered, how its sessions and decisions work through rough consensus, who plays which role, how disputes are appealed, and how documents move from drafts to RFCs.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo, not a standard. It has been obsoleted by RFC 2418 and updated by RFC 1871.

today: RFC 1603 is an Informational memo that has been obsoleted by RFC 2418 and updated by RFC 1871, so it describes the 1994 process rather than the current one.

sections.title: The IETF and Its Working Groups
sections.content:
The IETF develops and reviews specifications intended as Internet Standards. It is managed by the IESG (Internet Engineering Steering Group), whose members include an IETF Chair and the Area Directors, each responsible for a set of activities and working groups. At the time of writing there were 10 areas: User Services, Applications, Service Applications, Transport Services, Internet, Routing, Network Management, Operational Requirements, Security, and Standards & Processes.

The real work is done by working groups (WGs), of which the memo says there were more than 60. They tend to have a narrow focus and a lifetime bounded by a specific task. There is no formal membership in the IETF: participation is open to all, and people take part as individual technical contributors rather than as representatives of organizations.

The memo uses words like "shall", "must" and "is required" for essential steps, and "suggested", "should" and "may" for guidance that is strongly recommended but not essential. It leans on RFC 1602, the Internet Standards Process, for the philosophy behind it.
sections.eli5: The IETF is a huge open club of people who design how the Internet works. It splits its work into small teams called working groups, and anyone can join in.

sections.title: Forming a Working Group
sections.content:
A working group can start at the initiative of an Area Director or of individuals, but it needs the advice and consent of the relevant Area Director. The AD and the IESG weigh questions such as whether the goals are specific and achievable, whether the work overlaps another group, and whether there is enough interest and expertise. The memo says four or five active participants are typically required, and that a base of interested end users should exist.

Every group needs a charter, described as a contract between the group and the IETF. A charter has six parts: working group name (with an acronym of at most 8 printable ASCII characters), Chair(s) (one or two), area and Area Director, mailing list, a description of the group, and goals and milestones. Milestones must be concrete deliverables, such as "Internet-Draft finished", and the memo suggests setting them every 3 to 6 months. The IESG gives final approval and the IAB reviews all charters.

When it is unclear whether a topic merits a group, a Birds of a Feather (BOF) session can be held at an IETF meeting. A BOF needs the Area Director's approval and may be held only once, with a second meeting only in unusual circumstances; BOFs are not permitted to meet three times.
sections.eli5: To start a team, you write down its goals and deadlines in a charter, and the people in charge have to agree. If nobody is sure the team is needed, you first hold a one-time chat to find out.

sections.title: How Working Groups Operate
sections.content:
The core rule is that decisions come from rough consensus. This does not require everyone to agree, and the dominant view prevails, but dominance is not decided by volume or persistence. The memo says consensus can be found by balloting, humming, or any other means the group agrees on. Decisions reached at IETF meetings are not final until conveyed to the mailing list to verify consensus.

Much of the work happens on a public mailing list, and all working group actions shall be taken in a public forum. The Chair must publish a draft agenda well in advance, and sessions must have minutes with the agenda, the discussion and decisions, and an attendee list. A WG must make sure its process does not exclude email-only participants.

To keep things moving, the Chair may reject or defer input that is Old, Minor, out of Timing, or out of Scope. If someone thinks the process went wrong, appeals climb four levels in order: the WG Chair, the Area Director, the IESG, and finally the IAB.
sections.eli5: The team does not vote on everything. They go with what most people clearly agree on, and the person leading keeps the talk moving. If someone thinks it was unfair, they can ask bigger and bigger bosses to look again.

sections.title: Roles and Ending a Working Group
sections.content:
The WG Chair has wide discretion and is responsible for forward progress through a fair and open process. Duties include moderating the mailing list, organizing sessions, reporting results to the Area Director, spreading the workload, and working with the RFC Editor on publication. Other roles are the Editor/Secretary (records decisions rather than doing basic specification), the Facilitator (manages the style of discussion, not its content), and design teams, which may hold closed sessions but whose work must be open to review by the whole group.

The Area Director ensures coherent, coordinated and timely output from the groups in an area, handling planning, coordination, meeting schedules, reporting, reviewing and progress tracking. An Area Consultant, a senior participant, may be assigned to a working group, and an Area Directorate of senior technical people may be appointed to help review.

Groups are typically chartered for a specific task and disbanded when it is done. A group that produced a Proposed or Draft Standard becomes dormant instead, keeping its mailing list. A group that cannot finish can recharter to a smaller task, choose new Chairs, or disband.
sections.eli5: Each team has a leader who keeps things fair and moving, a note-taker, and a boss for the whole area. When the team finishes its job it closes down, but it may keep a mailing list open for questions.

sections.title: Working Group Documents
sections.content:
Relevant documents for a session should be published at least two weeks before it. Early work is shared as Internet-Drafts, which the memo stresses are working documents with no official standards status whatsoever; they may become standards-track documents or sink from sight.

Final results are published as RFCs, the archival record of the Internet community. The memo is explicit that the RFC series is only a publication mechanism: all Internet Standards are published as RFCs, but not all RFCs specify standards. Status comes from separate labels assigned by the IESG.

To publish, the Chair emails the Area Director, with a copy to the IESG Secretary, asking that the document be progressed as an Informational, Experimental, Prototype or standards-track RFC. Review can end in acceptance as is, requested changes, or rejection, which the memo expects to be unlikely for documents from a working group. Before a final decision on a standards-track document, the IESG Secretary issues a Last Call, a two-week period for final comments from the IETF.

Much of the document archive logistics (anonymous FTP and gopher servers at InterNIC, and an appendix with a sample charter for the Multiparty Multimedia Session Control group) reflect 1994 practice.
sections.eli5: Teams share rough drafts early, which are only ideas. When a draft is ready, the bosses give it a last public look for two weeks before it becomes an official RFC.

messages.label: Raise concern
messages.note: Always start closest to the group.

messages.label: Not satisfied: escalate
messages.note: Via the IESG Chair and the Standards & Processes AD.
